import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 4.2

by S. I. Adian

Find an infinite finitely generated group of exponent less than $100$. Do such
groups exist with exponent $5$?

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«4.2»

/--
Find an infinite finitely generated group of exponent less than $100$. The
positivity condition excludes the value $0$ that `Monoid.exponent` assigns to
groups having no finite exponent.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem parts.a :
    ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G) (_ : Infinite G) (_ : Group.FG G),
      0 < Monoid.exponent G ∧ Monoid.exponent G < 100 := by
  sorry

/--
Do there exist infinite finitely generated groups of exponent $5$? Here this
means that every element $g$ satisfies $g^5 = 1$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem parts.b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G) (_ : Infinite G) (_ : Group.FG G),
      ∀ g : G, g ^ 5 = 1 := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«4.2»

Part (b) states exponent 5 by the direct law `∀ g : G, g ^ 5 = 1`. For an infinite group this is equivalent to having exact `Monoid.exponent` equal to 5.
The group structure, infinitude, and finite-generation property are all existentially quantified, using Mathlib's existing `Infinite` and `Group.FG` classes.

by S. I. Adian

b) Do there exist such groups of exponent $5$?

This is the bounded Burnside problem for small exponents. The exponent of a group
$G$ is the least positive integer $n$ with $g^n = 1$ for all $g \in G$. In Mathlib,
`Monoid.exponent G` is this integer if it exists and `0` otherwise, so
"exponent $< 100$" is stated as `0 < Monoid.exponent G ∧ Monoid.exponent G < 100`.

*References:*
* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46), Problem 4.2
* [Burnside problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside_problem), Wikipedia
-/

/--
a) Find an infinite finitely generated group of exponent $< 100$.

Stated as the existence of an infinite finitely generated group $G$ whose exponent
$n$ satisfies $0 < n < 100$. The condition $0 < n$ excludes groups of infinite
exponent, for which `Monoid.exponent G = 0`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«4.2».parts.a :
    ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), Infinite G ∧ Group.FG G ∧
      0 < Monoid.exponent G ∧ Monoid.exponent G < 100 := by
  sorry

/--
b) Do there exist such groups of exponent $5$?

That is, does there exist an infinite finitely generated group of exponent $5$?
-/

theorem kourovka.«4.2».parts.b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), Infinite G ∧ Group.FG G ∧ Monoid.exponent G = 5 := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«4.2»

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 4.2

by S. I. Adian

a) Find an infinite finitely generated group of exponent $< 100$.

b) Do there exist such groups of exponent $5$?

A group $G$ has exponent $n$ if $n$ is the least positive integer with $g^n = 1$ for all
$g \in G$. The problem is the bounded Burnside problem for small exponents: infinite
finitely generated groups of exponent $n$ (the free Burnside groups $B(m, n)$, $m \geq 2$)
are known to exist for all odd $n \geq 665$ (Adian) and all $n \geq 8000$ (Lysenok), while
$B(m, n)$ is finite for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\}$.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«4.2»

/--
a) Find an infinite finitely generated group of exponent $< 100$.

Stated as the existence of an infinite finitely generated group $G$ together with an
integer $n$ with $0 < n < 100$ and $g^n = 1$ for all $g \in G$. This is equivalent to
$0 < \operatorname{exp}(G) < 100$ for the exponent $\operatorname{exp}(G)$ of $G$
(`Monoid.exponent G`, which is $0$ by convention when no such $n$ exists).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«4.2».parts.a :
    ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), Infinite G ∧ Group.FG G ∧
      ∃ n : ℕ, 0 < n ∧ n < 100 ∧ ∀ g : G, g ^ n = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
b) Do there exist such groups of exponent $5$?

That is, does there exist an infinite finitely generated group $G$ with $g^5 = 1$ for all
$g \in G$? Since an infinite group is non-trivial and $5$ is prime, this is the same as
$G$ having exponent exactly $5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«4.2».parts.b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), Infinite G ∧ Group.FG G ∧ ∀ g : G, g ^ 5 = 1 := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«4.2»
